rejected.title: Context and the writer's identity
card: Context is where and when a piece appears, and who it is meant for. A newspaper opinion page, a school assembly and a social media post can each shape how the same words are heard.
The writer's identity is who they are and what they do, such as a doctor, a politician or a teenager. It can affect how far an audience trusts or accepts what they say.

A writer's identity can give the argument authority, as when a nurse writes about hospital staffing. It can also make an audience doubt the writer's motives, as when a company owner argues for lower company taxes.
In an analysis, name the publication or setting and the writer's role. Then explain how each is likely to position the intended audience.
rejected.remember: Where a piece appears and who wrote it can shape how the audience responds.

a.q: A piece about ambulance delays is written by a long-serving paramedic. How might her identity affect readers?
opts: It may lead readers to trust her view on ambulance care
It may tell readers where and when the piece appeared
It may turn her contention into a proven fact for readers
It may stop readers seeing the piece as an argument
a.why: Years of work as a paramedic can give her authority on ambulance care, so readers may be more willing to trust her. Where and when a piece appears is its context, not the writer's identity. Her role can shape how readers react, but her contention is still an argument, not a proven fact.
a.clue: Think about how readers respond to someone with experience in the topic.

b.q: Dev owns a chain of gyms. He writes an opinion piece in a local paper arguing that councils should cut fees for sports facilities. How might his identity affect some readers?
opts: Some may doubt his motives, as he could gain from the change
Some may find the argument stronger, as he is not affected
Some may see the piece as neutral, as it is in a newspaper
Some may ignore the contention, as he is a business owner
b.why: A gym owner could benefit from cheaper facility fees, so some readers may suspect self-interest. The newspaper setting does not make the piece neutral, because an opinion page presents a personal view. His role may lead readers to question him, but it does not make them ignore the contention.
b.clue: Ask who might gain if the audience agrees with Dev.
